author: ch402
text:
Advertising based business models also do this implicitly -- I assume showing ads to rich people is worth more than showing ads to poor people, and implicitly funds poorer market segments?

(This seems like an underrated point in favor of their societal value.)

author: ch402
text: And it seems like companies have been developing better business models for high fixed-cost, zero-margin products. Software companies having a decent free version of their product seems common in a way that it didn't 15 years ago?

author: ch402
text: Sometimes society seems to accomplish this by selectively not enforcing copyright. (And in some cases, it may actually be the case that the companies want that!)

author: ch402
text: But as a society, we want companies to not waste all this value! From a global perspective, not reaching lower-paying market segments is at best a waste, and at worst a moral tragedy.

author: ch402
text: Why don't they? There might not be a way for a company to segment their product to reach lower-paying segments without reducing the amount of value they can extract from higher-paying segments. Or it might be really hard.

author: ch402
text: But presumably companies would segment their products to reach every part of the market if they easily could. If only for the advertising and good will.

author: ch402
text: "You have a responsibility to reach my market segment (which can't spend much on music). If you aren't reaching us, you're just pointlessly depriving us of something important, and we don't consider you to be upholding the social contract behind copyright."

author: ch402
text: It seems like you could frame part of the debate over the copyright of music this way. People are upset because it seems unfair to deprive them of access to music when they'd never have paid for it, and thus the company incurs no loss.

author: ch402
text: But it seems like more mild versions of this exist everywhere. If someone truly can't afford to pay, and there's zero marginal cost to giving them something, there's something ugly and wasteful about not giving it to them, even if it's something like entertainment.

author: ch402
text:
This is clearly an ethical issue in the case of drugs. Pharmaceutical companies need to recoup expenses by charging some groups, but we don't want people who can't afford to pay to not be treated!

(Often drugs cost much less in poor countries, a kind of segmentation.)

author: ch402
text: These issues become especially striking for things with a high fixed cost, and a low-marginal cost. A typical software company needs to charge some group a bunch of money, but could give everyone else their product for free if it didn't disrupt that.

author: ch402
text: Market segmentation example: Both hobbyists and professionals are interested in a product, but professionals are willing to pay way more. Ideally a company finds a way to create a "hobby version" and "professional version", charging a lot more for the professional version.

author: ch402
text: (Caveat: I don't know much about business / economics / etc. Just random shower thoughts on something I'm not an expert on.)

author: ch402

Market segmentation (as I understand it) is a standard business thing where companies group potential buyers and target them differently.

It seems to me that market segmentation is often a moral issue as well as a business one, but people don't usually discuss it that way?

text: I was surprised that IVF (not including egg freezing) only seems to be worth starting 1-3 years earlier in one’s mid-30s, according to Habbema. Of course, that’s still a great blessing to those it helps, but I’d hoped it was more. https://t.co/w27gBVimmy

author: ch402
text: The Habbema data also suggests starting a single year earlier can matter a shocking amount: there are points where the likelihood of achieving a desired family size drops 10%/year! https://t.co/LnLa8wAeWY

author: ch402
text: (For example, if one wants to have 3 children, one typically needs to start 5-7 years earlier to have the same probability of achieving that goal as someone having a single child.)

author: ch402
text: My biggest takeaway from  Habbema is that the number of children you want to have seems to have an enormous effect on things. This feels obvious in retrospect, but seems really important. https://t.co/9SQ7whZD6M

author: ch402
text: Here’s the overall visualization of the Habbema data I found most useful. For a given maternal age, what is the largest family size (up to 3) that one can achieve with a given probability? https://t.co/PZqeu4Svlu

author: ch402
text:
Another big caveat: while Habbema et al have an IVF version of their model, they don't consider egg freezing. I expect egg freezing changes the picture a lot, and is increasingly common, so it's a really big limitation!

With all of that said...

author: ch402
text: To be really clear: I’m not an expert. I’m not qualified to evaluate the Habbema paper. I may have misunderstood things. I did this analysis as a tiny, fast side project. I had to extract data from line plots. Please don’t draw too much from this.

author: ch402
text: But it didn’t include a lot of analysis I wanted. So I extracted the data and did my own rough analysis. I'm sharing this very rough work in case it's useful to anyone, but please take it with a big grain of salt!

author: ch402
text: Many fertility papers report statistics which are actually kind of subtle to interpret. Habbema handles those details for us and provides a model for the question "what are my chances of having N children at a given age?" for a typical case.

author: ch402
text: Habbema et al's "Realizing a desired family size: when should couples start?" (https://t.co/C5GbkoIE5q) is a really helpful paper for this.

author: ch402
text: (There’s sometimes an attitude that men don’t need to worry about how age affects fertility. I think this is mistaken. Even if the direct effect of paternal age is often small, if my partner’s age is correlated with mine, these statistics have a profound *indirect* effect on me!)

author: ch402
text: I really want to have children someday (https://t.co/4i8CKJIVd9 ). As I’ve started to get closer to my 30s, I wanted to have an accurate picture of how age affects fertility.

quoted.text:
Five of my close friends will soon be parents. I feel very excited for them. I also feel a bit sad: I really want to have a family myself someday and it feels far away.
 
We don’t talk very much about men wanting to have children, so I thought a thread might be positive.

text: Saying things like “I hope that you’re well” or “you’re in my thoughts” just feels so incredibly inadequate. Religious traditions seem to express this feeling much more strongly, and I enjoy Gilead’s reflection on it.

author: ch402
text: There are more positive versions. I often just wish so much for someone to succeed, to find happiness, for things to go well for them. A close friend had a child last week and despite not having yet met them, I wish so much good for that child.

author: ch402
text: Similarly, one might desperately hope for family in another country to be okay during COVID. Or for a friend going into a serious surgery to be well. And in those moments, for all the intensity of our feelings, we’re powerless.

author: ch402
text: For example, in a breakup, one might care intensely about their partner and feel a profound desire for them to be well, but separation makes you powerless to help.

author: ch402
text: Some of my most intense emotional experiences have been intensely wishing for someone to be well and simultaneously being utterly powerless to help them.

author: ch402

text: It also seems -- and this is really my speculation at this point -- to influence precipitation on the coasts of continents. The sea produces humidity, land (and especially mountains) produces rain shadows. https://t.co/PNG828l2fK

author: ch402
text: Air in different Hadley cells moving East or West explains the trajectory of hurricanes. They form near the equator and so first move West (into the East side of continents). If they drift up to 30° they then curve East. https://t.co/VPK75Su0pG

author: ch402
text: (Why does Earth have 3 Hadley cells per hemisphere instead of 1 or 5? The primary reason is the coriolis effect bending the path of air on that length scale. So the number of Hadley cells a planet has is determined by its radius and its rotation speed. https://t.co/0L4h2ibiFv )

author: ch402
text: More generally, air tends to move East or West in each Hadley cell. https://t.co/ipTXIexgTy

author: ch402
text: But why do hurricanes move West? Wind near the equator systematically blows west due to an interaction between Hadley cells and the coriolis effect. https://t.co/067Q6pNlQA

author: ch402
text: Imagine you were standing in the middle of a merry-go-round and threw a ball. From your perspective, the ball's trajectory would seem to curve. Now imagine doing the same thing at the North pole. The Earth is spinning like the merry-go-round, so the path would curve. https://t.co/740XyaRBZ7

author: ch402
text: To answer this question, we’ll need to understand the coriolis effect. (This will also explain why hurricanes spin different directions in each hemisphere! And why each pole has a permanent wind pattern that looks like a hurricane spinning in reverse!)

author: ch402
text:
A first answer is that hurricanes form near the equator and move East, generally hitting the west side of continents. If they last long enough and drift away from the equator, they later curve West (eg. Europe is sometimes hit by the weakened remnants of hurricanes). 

But why? https://t.co/D8Mjd1Sh9l

author: ch402
text:
That’s three mysteries down, one more to go:

Why do hurricanes ten to hit the east coast, rather than the west coast, of continents? For example, why are Florida and Japan so affected by hurricanes, when California and Spain are not?

author: ch402
text: (You may notice places where winter vs summer humidity are the opposite of what this explanation predicts, especially on the East or West coasts of continents. Our final mystery will shed light!)

author: ch402
text: A very cool animation of long-term mean precipitation by month, by PZmaps on Wikipedia https://t.co/IbR7eEP4EC

author: ch402
text: A more detailed diagram of (my understanding of!) what happens as the solar equator migrates. https://t.co/BHYEHy6jna

author: ch402
text: Over the course of the year, the solar equator migrates, stretching and compressing Hadley cells. If you’re in between the equator and 30°, you tend to have wetter summers. If you’re between 30° and 60°, wetter winters. https://t.co/UqTbp8SOZw

author: ch402
text: Returning to Earth, we’ve explained why some latitudes tend to be dry and some tend to be wet. But why does San Francisco (or the Mediterranean) have wet winters and dry summers, while India and Mexico tend to have wet summers and dry winters?

author: ch402
text: This allows us to answer why Jupiter has stripes. They correspond to Hadley cells with regions where air goes up being one color, and down another. Since it is much larger than Earth, there are more stripes! (It also spins faster, which we’ll see plays a large role as well.)

author: ch402
text:
Imagine making the Earth larger while magically holding everything else fixed.
 
The number of cells is discrete, so it seems like there must be a point where you jump to 5 cells, discontinuously moving the dry zones from ~90°/3 to ~90°/5.
 
A planetary scale phase change! 🤯

author: ch402
text: But why doesn’t the Earth just have one giant cell per hemisphere like Venus? We’ll return to the exact reasons later, but there are reasons that cells can’t be too big. Thus, larger planets tend to have more cells, and smaller planets fewer cells.

author: ch402
text:
If the three cells are of equal size, the space between should be 90°/3. (30° isn't arbitrary!!) So we should expect: 
 
Equator - Air rises causing lots of rain
30° - Dry air falls (it lost a lot of water on the way up!)
60° - Air rises, causing moderate rain
Poles - Air falls

author: ch402
text: George Hadley, who first proposed this general idea, thought air went from the equator all the way to the poles and back. This does happen on some planets, but on Earth each hemisphere has three “cells.” (Larger numbers are also possible, but must be odd.) https://t.co/HxaAS5QeOt

author: ch402
text:
The rising and falling air create pressure changes, and need to go somewhere or get replaced. For example, air is pulled towards the equator at ground level, and pushed away high up in the atmosphere. The opposite happens at the poles.

But what happens in between? https://t.co/BOixGws8Cl

author: ch402
text:
So, why is this? Notice:

(1) Air is warmest at the equator and should rise at the equator (and correspondingly, fall at the poles).
(2) The rising air at the equator will cool as it rises, causing rain. So we should expect the equator to be very wet! https://t.co/gg1t79qPUF

text: Someday I’ll get to have a family, and that will be lovely. But the present is also lovely, and it’s good to keep perspective on that.

author: ch402
text: (4) Being a parent through COVID seems like it would have been exceptionally challenging. Watching colleagues with kids, I feel very fortunate to have escaped that timing.

author: ch402
text: (3) I also try to remember that there are advantages to this stage of my life. I can structure my day how I want. I can hyper-focus on research. Under normal circumstances, I can go to a gym or a cafe early in the morning.

author: ch402
text: (2) I’d much, much rather wait to have kids with the right person. As much as it can feel lonely to wait, having children and then having a relationship not work out seems awful.

author: ch402
text: (I often emotionally focus on friends and colleagues getting married and having children. It’s easy to miss that they’re generally quite a bit older than me. Also, women often have these events happen at a younger age, so I shouldn't compare.)

author: ch402
text: (1) Taking a while to have kids is completely normal and expected. The median age for college educated men having a child is 33. I’d bet that for men with research careers it’s even later. https://t.co/l4EVY67bbg

author: ch402
text: Even if it isn’t that unusual, intensely wanting to have a family and having it feel far off can be kind of demoralizing and lonely. Here are a few things I try to keep in mind:

author: ch402
text: 4x is a large difference, but it isn’t _that_ big a difference. I’d guess there’s a lot of men who really want to have families but don’t talk about it very much.

author: ch402
text: So, how unusual is it? Rotkirch 2007 reports that in Finland,  ~6% of men in their 20s “often” have a “strong wish” to have a child compared to ~22% of women in the same age group. The ratio reduces as people get older, from ~4x 20-29s to ~1.5x 50-59. https://t.co/xQqSmbZgpy

author: ch402
text: It’s tempting to think that I’m at the extreme of the “men wanting to have children” distribution. (An ex described me as baby crazy, and there’s some truth to that!) But I think it’s also probably the case that most men who really want to have kids don’t talk about it very much.

author: ch402
text: I daydream about having kids. I read sappy fiction where people have babies. Sometimes I think I want to be a stay-at-home parent someday when I have kids. Before the pandemic, I’d sometimes babysit for fun.

author: ch402
text: I don’t think I have anything particularly insightful to say, but it feels like there’s probably some value simply in normalizing men intensely wanting to have families.

author: ch402

author: ch402

author: ch402

author: ch402

author: ch402
text:
I also feel like magic often gets at a desire for our feelings to *fundamentally* matter. 

When I feel deep emotions, it feels as though they *ought* to directly affect the world, but they don’t. In many fantasy worlds, emotions are reified first class objects.

author: ch402
text:
I think the crucial thing is that I imagine magic as *humane* and *intimate*, while technology is often *alienating* and *distant* in practice.

The Force is compelling because who doesn’t want to be profoundly directly connected to the universe?

author: ch402
text:
Another possible answer is that we’re deadened to the wonder of technology and science. We’ve lost our sense of awe (see https://t.co/gVqqIJAaCs). If magic existed, it might lose awe too.

I think that’s closer to true, but something is still missing.

author: ch402
text:
The easy answer is that magic is a power fantasy: it would give one power or make one special.

But that doesn’t really ring true to me.  I imagine magic being compelling if everyone had it. Conversely, not all fantastical powers I could imagine are emotionally resonant.

text: I’m generally pro moving to another environment once you’ve reflected a lot on what you’re interested in and have something you feel very actively excited about.

author: ch402
text: Antidote: Either (1) move to an environment which is aligned with your interests, or (2) temporarily buy into the interests of your group and try to exercise good taste within those interests.

author: ch402
text: This can happen even when those around you nominally support you working on whatever you’re interested in. It can be challenging to pursue a direction when people around you are unenthusiastic.

author: ch402
text: This generally leads to ideas optimized for compromise rather than quality. This both leads to lower quality work and deprives them of the opportunity to hone taste.

author: ch402
text:
Failure mode 3: Environment not aligned with your interests.

I sometimes talk to PhD students who have different interests than their advisor, and are trying to contort their research interests into something their advisor will find palatable.

author: ch402
text: Antidote: Help someone else with their project in a space you’re interested in. You’ll learn a lot and get your hands dirty without becoming overly committed to working on something long term. Ideally, by not leading the project, this should also be lower stress.

author: ch402
text: Sometimes people fall into a trap of trying to pick the perfect problem or have a brilliant insight before getting their hands dirty. You can’t have research taste in a vacuum. You need theoretical knowledge and research intimacy (https://t.co/sJrGuXI0ft ).

quoted.text: Research Intimacy: Internalizing obscure knowledge, equations, relationships, and ways of thinking related to a research topic.

author: ch402
text:
Failure mode 2: Lack of research knowledge / intimacy.

Theoretical knowledge is table stakes for research taste. You can’t have research taste in a vacuum.

author: ch402
text: Antidote: Set aside a week or two to step back and create a list of the other directions you think would be most promising to work on (look at new work, talk to others, etc). Then ask what you’d want to work on if you were starting from scratch. Repeat every 1-2 years as needed.

author: ch402
text:
Failure Mode 1: Getting overly attached to one research direction / falling into sunk costs.

A lot of researchers start working on one problem (often more due to circumstance than contemplated decision) and then find it hard to move on.

author: ch402
text: I also wanted to go through some research taste failure modes:

author: ch402
text:
Exercise 5: Critically consider your research taste, and the community taste around you. Your taste is likely very influenced by your research cluster (collaborators, advisor, etc).

eg. In what ways has your own research taste or your community's taste been wrong in the past?

author: ch402
text:
Exercise 4: Read books about the history of science. Reflect on why some researchers focused on important directions their contemporaries ignored.

(Kuhn’s “The Structure of Scientific Revolutions” is one of my favorite books, and you can get an audio book!)

author: ch402
text:
Exercise 3: Interview researchers around you on their taste. Why do they work on the problems they do? How do they pick problems? What’s their “big picture” of research?

Bonus: If you have a great interview, you might consider writing it up with their permission.

author: ch402
text: If you’re investing in brainstorming, you’ll have tens or hundreds of research ideas for each one you try. It can be emotionally uncomfortable when someone publishes an idea you had, but it’s an opportunity to get precious feedback for free.

author: ch402
text: Exercise 2: Pay attention when other people try ideas you’ve had. How did the results compare with your expectations?

author: ch402
text:
Exercise 1: Write down a list of research ideas. Have a mentor you respect rate each idea 1-10. Discuss ideas where you disagree with them after reflection.

It often takes several months of work to truly test an idea. Asking a mentor is a cheap proxy.
